attributes.title: Level 1

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create a new variable for both of your sprites?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

﻿

Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is it important to use descriptive sprite names, instead of leaving it “mySprite”?

❓ Why do you think the [stay in screen] block is important to a Player’s experience?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide the ninja to notice that the order of the code blocks matters. Any block that refers to a sprite needs to come after its [set sprite to] block.
steps.instructions:
Code a Player and an Enemy sprite.


Use the code block in the [on start] container block to create a Player sprite that moves with the direction buttons and stays in screen. Add an Enemy sprite, and set its sprite kind. Set the Enemy sprite’s position.


Remember to set the sprite’s variable by giving each sprite a unique name. 


Click ▶ to see both sprites show up on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the Enemy sprite to follow the Player sprite by updating the sprite names and adjusting the parameter?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens if the Enemy sprite’s speed is too high in the [set sprite follow] block? What if it’s too low?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 While the Enemy sprite doesn’t have to be at the exact coordinates shown, it is important to have it reasonably far from the Player sprite.
steps.instructions:
Set the Enemy sprite to follow the Player sprite.


Adjust the Enemy sprite’s speed by clicking the + in the [set sprite follow] block to edit the speed parameter. Try out different numbers until you find one that is challenging, but not impossible.


Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprite follow the Player sprite.

steps.hints: ❓Did you drag the Food sprite’s code blocks to the top of the [on start] container block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓Did you rename the new sprite variable?

❓ Where should you place the Food sprite’s code so that it appears behind the Player and Enemy sprites?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to ninjas that sprite kinds can be used to identify sprites and decide what events happen, and “Food” is a generic category for something that the Player is collecting or looking for.
steps.instructions:
Add a new sprite kind for the Player sprite to collect!


Add a new sprite, then set the sprite kind to “Food”. Set the position of the Food sprite, too.


Drag the Food sprite’s code blocks to the top of the [on start] container so that it appears behind the Player and Enemy sprites.


Click ▶ to see the Food sprite appear!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you rename each Food sprite and give each of them a unique position?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution: 


Ask the ninja:

❓Have all of the new sprites been set to the correct sprite kind?

❓Did you place each Food sprite in a unique position on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to consider the sequence of the sprites so that all the Food sprites appear behind the Player and Enemy sprites.

💡Guide ninjas to duplicate the Food sprite’s [set sprite to] and [set sprite position] blocks by right clicking, and selecting “Duplicate”. This will create a copy of that block with all the same parameters. Prompt the ninja to update the sprite name and position in each block.
steps.instructions:
Add more Food sprites for the Player to collect! 


Right click to duplicate the Food sprite’s [set sprite to] block, then give the new Food sprite variable a new name. Set a different position for each new Food sprite, too.


Click ▶ to see all the Food sprites appear at once., and test out what happens when the Player sprite overlaps them!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you drag the otherSprite bubble into the [set sprite image to] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

﻿Ask the ninja:

❓ Which sprite kind should you update—the first or second? What should you update it to?

❓ Did the program work as expected? Does each Food sprite respond to overlapping the Player sprite in the way you expected it to?

❓ Did you select a different image for the Food sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip: 

💡 Prompt ninjas to consider why the use of the “otherSprite” bubble is important. Because there are numerous Food sprites in the project, using the “otherSprite” bubble allows the ninja to access the exact sprite being overlapped by a Player sprite. If a specific sprite name were used in the [set sprite image to] block, the code inside the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container would only run if that exact sprite were overlapped by a Player sprite.

💡 Encourage ninjas to test out the code in the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container. What happens when the Player sprite hovers over a Food sprite for an extended period of time? Does the sound continue to play?
steps.instructions:
Make something happen when the Player and Food sprites touch - or overlap - on screen! 


Drag out an [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block, and change the second sprite kind to “Food”.


When the sprites overlap, the Food sprite should change its image, and then play a sound. Drag a [set sprite image to] block into the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container. Drag the “otherSprite” bubble into the sprite name parameter, then update the image parameter of the [set sprite image to] block. 


By using the “otherSprite” bubble in the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container, all of the new Food sprites will respond the same way when they overlap with the Player sprite.


Add a [play sound] block into the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container. Allow the sound to play [until done].


Click ▶ to see each Food sprite image change when it's overlapped by the Player sprite!

steps.hints: ❓Did you drag a [change score by] block into the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution: 


Ask the ninja:

❓Did the score appear on the top right corner?

❓What happens now, when the Player sprite overlaps a Food sprite? What happens when the Player sprite continues to overlap a Food sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Though the [change score by] block can work in this activity without the [set score to] block, it is good to get in the habit of setting a variable at the beginning of the program.

💡Prompt the ninja to notice that the score continues to increase while the Player sprite overlaps a Food sprite. The sprites need to be separated (or destroyed, in the next step) to discontinue the overlap event.
steps.instructions:
Add a score variable to this game!


Open the Info code block menu, and drag a [set score to] block into the [on start] container block, then set the parameter to 0.


Open the Info code block menu, and drag a [change score by] block into the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block. 


Click ▶ to see the score change when the Player sprite overlaps with the Food sprite!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you drag the otherSprite bubble into the  [destroy sprite] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:❓ Did you drag the “otherSprite” bubble into the parameter of the [destroy sprite] block? ❓ What happens now when the Player overlaps with the Food sprite?

Sensei Pro Tip:💡The bug happens because the score continues changing for as long as the sprites are overlapping. Once the sprite is destroyed, the score will stop changing.
steps.instructions:
Oh no, there is a bug! When the Player sprite overlaps with the Food sprite, the score increases by more than 1! 


Code the Food sprite to disappear when the Player sprite overlaps with it. Open the Sprites code block menu and drag out a [destroy sprite] block into the bottom of the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container. Drag the (otherSprite) bubble into the parameter of the [destroy sprite] block. 


Click ▶ to see the Food sprite disappear after the score increases. By immediately removing the overlapped Food sprite, the overlap event will stop, causing the score to only increase by 1.

steps.hints: ❓Did you update the parameter in the [change score by] block so that the score goes down by 1 whenever the Player sprite overlaps with the Enemy sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓What two sprite kinds are you coding an overlap for?

❓Did you select Enemy for the second sprite kind?

❓Which block will change the score?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to duplicate the original Enemy sprite’s [set sprite position] block if they want the x y coordinates to reset to the exact starting position.
steps.instructions:
Make something happen when the Player sprite overlaps with the Enemy sprite.


Drag out another [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block, and change the second sprite kind to Enemy. Drag a [change score by] block into the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container and change the parameter to -1.


Use a [set sprite position to] block to move the Enemy sprite back to its starting position after it overlaps the Player sprite to avoid losing more than 1 point!


Click ▶ to see the score decrease and the Enemy reset its position when the Player sprite overlaps with the Enemy sprite.

steps.hints: ❓Did you add the [use effect] block to the top of the [on countdown end] container, before the [game over] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution: 

﻿

Ask the ninja:

❓Did you set the parameter in the [start countdown] block?

❓Did you set the [game over] toggle to WIN?

❓ Where should you place the [use effect] block so it changes the [game over] effect?

❓What else might happen when the countdown ends?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to try out different amounts of time to make the game exciting but not too short.

💡Guide ninjas to place the [use effect] block above the [game over] block so it changes the effect before the game over code runs. This is similar to changing the dialog frame before using a [show long text] block.
steps.instructions:
Add a timer to make the game even more exciting!


Open the Info code block menu, then drag a [start countdown] block into the [on start] container block. Set the parameter to be the number of seconds you want the game to last.


Then, open the Info code block menu and drag out an [on countdown end] container block. Add [game over] and [use effect] blocks into the [on countdown end] container, set the toggle to WIN, and add a fun win effect.


Click ▶ to see the timer countdown as you play the game!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add customizations to your game including a background color, screen effect, directions and more?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:❓Which block will set a background color? Which block will set screen effects? Which block will set dialog boxes?❓What directions will help people understand how your project works?

Sensei Pro Tip:💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall.
steps.instructions:
Customize this game by setting a background and adding a screen effect, adding directions with dialog boxes, and making other things happen when sprites overlap!


Click ▶ to see the completed game project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a game in which points increase as the Player sprite “collects” as many Food sprites as possible while staying away from the Enemy sprite!

validationItems.text: Create 1 Player sprite, 1 Enemy sprite, at least 3 Food sprites
Set the Enemy sprite to follow the Player sprite
Change the Food sprite image, play a sound, change the score, then destroy the Food sprite when the Player sprite overlaps it
When the Player sprite overlaps the Enemy sprite, change the score variable and reset the Enemy sprite’s position.
Set the game to end in a win with a game over effect when the countdown timer reaches 0
Customize the game with backgrounds, effects, text boxes, sounds, and speech bubbles

attributes.description: Welcome to Level 1 of Yellow Belt! In this level, you’ll learn about variables, which are pieces of data that can be stored, updated, and used in your programs. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 1:

badges.title: Data Entry
badges.description: Use variables to keep track of data in a project.

badges.title: YOLO
badges.description: Set and change the lives variable in a project.

badges.title: Time Flies
badges.description: Set a countdown timer in a project.

badges.title: Keeping Track
badges.description: Set and change the score variable in a project.

badges.title: -poof-
badges.description: Destroy a sprite when something happens in a project.
